A study compared the efficacy of two types of multiple micronutrient supplements, Sprinkles and Foodlets, against the standard recommended supplement (Drops) in Iranian infants. The findings were published in the Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2009. 2. Research conducted in two rural districts of Indonesia evaluated the impact of fortifying cooking oil with vitamin A on the vitamin A status of mothers and children. This study was documented in 2015. 3. The introduction of red palm oil into a supplementary feeding program, specifically the 'ready-to-eat' format, was assessed through the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) in India. The results were published in the Indian Journal of Public Health in 1999. 4. A study in Ghana demonstrated that a complementary food supplement fortified with macroand micronutrients significantly increased plasma branched-chain amino acid levels in infants. This research was published in the Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2017. 5. A trial in Niger investigated the preventive effects of long-term supplementation with two nutritious food supplements on young children. The results, focusing on growth and health outcomes, were published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 6. A study in North India examined the compliance and effectiveness of home-based fortification strategies for delivering iron and zinc to children aged 6–24 months. The impact on hematological and growth markers was reported in the Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition in 2014. 7. Research on Nias Island, Indonesia, compared locally produced cereal/nut/legume-based biscuits with peanut/milk-based spreads for treating moderately to mildly wasted children. The study highlighted issues of acceptance and compliance and was published in the Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015. 8. A pilot study in Guinea-Bissau evaluated the effectiveness of two ready-to-use supplementary foods (RUSFs) with varying dairy protein content on the growth and nutritional status of young children. The findings were presented in the FASEB Journal in 2015. 9. A randomized controlled trial in Guinea-Bissau demonstrated the benefits of a higher dairy supplement in reducing wasting among mothers and its differential impact on infants and children. The study was published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2017. 10. A synthesis of three randomized controlled trials in Guinea-Bissau revealed that higher levels of dairy in supplements improved physical outcomes in children aged 6–59 months, adolescents aged 5–19 years, and mothers. The findings were published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2018. 11. A study from 1995 explored age-related differences in the impact of nutritional supplementation on growth, with findings published in the Journal of Nutrition. 12. A placebo-controlled intervention trial in Cambodia assessed the efficacy and safety of twice-weekly administration of iron and folic acid, with or without additional micronutrients, in anemic infants aged 6–24 months. The results were published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2009. 13. A double-blinded randomized controlled trial investigated the modification of dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids through complementary food enhancements to promote n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid synthesis in healthy infants. The findings were published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2009. 14. A study in a food aid-dependent refugee population demonstrated that maize meal fortification improved vitamin A and iron status in adolescents and reduced childhood anemia. The results were published in Public Health Nutrition in 2008. 15. A cluster-randomized controlled trial in rural Bangladesh evaluated the variable impact of fortified lipid-based and blended complementary foods on body composition in children. The findings were published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2020. 16. A study in Mexico compared the efficacy of ferrous gluconate and ferrous sulfate added to complementary food distributed by the Oportunidades nutrition program in reducing iron deficiency in toddlers. The results were published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2008. 17. A randomized controlled trial in India assessed the effectiveness of indigenous ready-to-use therapeutic food in community-based management of uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition. The findings were published in the Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 2013. 18. A study in Cambodia developed and evaluated the acceptability of locally made fish-based ready-to-use products for preventing and treating malnutrition. The findings were published in the Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2018. 19. A four-country randomized trial investigated the effect of early, short-term supplementation on the weight and linear growth of infants aged 4–7 months in developing countries. The results were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1996. 20. A study in Burkina Faso evaluated the efficacy of Spirulina and Misola in the nutritional rehabilitation of undernourished children. The findings were published in the Nutrition Journal in 2006. 21. A randomized controlled trial in India assessed the effectiveness of locally made ready-to-use therapeutic food for treating malnutrition. The findings were published in Indian Pediatrics in 2010. 22. The WinFood project in Cambodia evaluated the effects of animal-source foods and micronutrient-fortified complementary foods on body composition, linear growth, and iron status. The findings were published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2013. 23. A randomized trial in Cambodia assessed the effects of animal-source food and micronutrient fortification in complementary food products on body composition, iron status, and linear growth. The findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015. 24. A clinical trial in Malawi demonstrated that including whey protein and whey permeate in ready-to-use supplementary food improved recovery rates in children with moderate acute malnutrition. The findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016. 25. A cluster-randomized trial evaluated the impact of a package of health and nutrition services on sustained recovery in children after moderate acute malnutrition. The findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2017. 26. A study in Guatemala assessed the acceptability of a fortified atole among children attending daycare centers and its effects on linear growth and hemoglobin status. The findings were presented in the FASEB Journal in 2016. 27. A field trial in Thailand evaluated the impact of supplementary feeding on hill-tribe children aged 1–4 years over a one-year follow-up period. The findings were published in the Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand.
